title: Why One 'Quick Message Check' Can Cost You 23 Minutes
alt_title_1: The Cognitive Tax Behind 'Just Checking Slack for 10 Seconds'
alt_title_2: Sophie Leroy's Attention Residue Study Will Change How You Work
description_hook: Checking a notification for 30 seconds never costs just 30 seconds. Sophie Leroy's attention residue research and Gloria Mark's interruption studies explain why, and the simple physical rule to fix it.

scenes.headline: A 30-Second Glance Costs 23 Minutes
bullets: Quick message checks feel harmless in the moment
Gloria Mark: ~23 minutes on average to resume an interrupted task
scenes.narration: Glancing at a single notification for thirty seconds does not cost you thirty seconds. Gloria Mark's research found it takes about twenty-three minutes on average to get back to an interrupted task.
scenes.source: Gloria Mark et al., 'The Cost of Interrupted Work', CHI (2008)

scenes.headline: Prof. Sophie Leroy's Attention Residue Lab
bullets: Your brain cannot snap cleanly between unfinished tasks
Part of your attention stays on the message you just read
scenes.narration: In 2009, business professor Sophie Leroy showed why. She called it attention residue. When you switch from deep work to check one message, part of your attention stays stuck behind.
scenes.source: Sophie Leroy, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes (2009)

scenes.headline: Why 4 Quick Checks Ruin an Entire Morning
scenes.left_body: Check inbox every 15m -> permanent cognitive static
scenes.right_body: Zero open loops -> 100% bandwidth on 1 high-value asset
scenes.narration: Even after you look back at your main task, your brain operates with a steep cognitive penalty while clearing that leftover residue. Four quick checks in two hours means zero deep output.

scenes.headline: The Out-of-Sight 90-Minute Protocol
scenes.stat_subtext: Phone in another room -> 3x faster asset output
scenes.narration: Use the Out-of-Sight Protocol: place your phone inside a closed drawer in another room for one ninety-minute block every morning before opening email.

scenes.headline: Guard the Seal on Your First 90 Minutes
bullets: Physical distance beats willpower every morning
Ship one real asset before opening any inbox
scenes.narration: One uninterrupted ninety-minute sprint can beat a whole fragmented workday.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule of thumb (advice, not a study)
